utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Thursday, January 21st, 2010, and I greet our accused, Defence counsel, all members of the OTP in the courtroom, and everyone helping us. I believe that the Registrar has some IC numbers for us. He has the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. Thank you. 4D has submitted their response to the Prosecution's objections to their list of exhibits tendered through Witness Vinko Maric. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01162. The Prosecution has also submitted their response to 2D and 4D's objections to their documents tendered via Witness Vinko Maric. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01163 and 01164 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Kruger, you have the floor. I believe you had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everybody in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, simply to introduce a new member of the Prosecution team, whom you'll see sitting in court with us today. Ms. Jelena Vladisavljev has joined us, and she recently completed her studies at the Novi Sad -- legal studies at the Novi Sad University, and she's with us for a few months as an intern. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I greet her on behalf of the Trial Chamber, and I wish her the best during her internship with the OTP. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I also wanted to say that I forgot to greet our witness. Colonel, good afternoon. I hadn't forgotten you in thought, but it's not on the transcript, so I believe it has to be noted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Brigadier Jasak.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us finish our discussion concerning Mr. Misic. First question: Was he a charismatic person, in a way, in respect to the resistance that was being built up in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, he was a charismatic person of the resistance against aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, when was he killed and how? Do people know how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, my commander, Tihomir Misic, was killed on the 16th of May, 1992, while touring positions that were held by Croats and, on the other side, Muslims. I know that firing started from the positions that were held by Muslims. That's what was said. I was present during the post-mortem, and I saw that there were four different types of ammunition in the body of my late commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it correct that this gentleman was well liked both among the Croats and the Muslims as one of the initiators of the resistance in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, that is absolutely true, because in that area where the Old Bridge is, where we held positions, we had these people from Mahala there who were personally armed by Tihomir Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How did that piece of news resound in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It caused a great shock in Mostar, concern as to how we would defend ourselves now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What was I at that time for Mostar and Capljina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have we ever met, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, was the murder of Mr. Misic ever fully investigated?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I have no knowledge to that effect; namely, that that murder was fully investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: During those days in Mostar, how many casualties were there in Mostar because of the bombing? Please tell Their Honours who is attacking, who is bombing, how many wounded there are, how many killed persons there are, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time, from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, there were shellings every day from Slipcici at the town of Mostar. There were many casualties among soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to that road. You mentioned the road across Goranci. Is that the only road through which one could leave Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before talking about the road, let me return to the subject of Tihomir Misic. I might have misunderstood because you were speaking extremely fast, but I thought I understood that he died on May 16, 1992, whilst he was touring or inspecting the lines, and, at the time, he was with Muslims and he was shot at. Is this what happened? And according to you, he was shot at from the Muslim lines. I would like to know whether, when he was killed, he was escorted by Muslim soldiers of the Mostar Battalion. Were they alongside with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on that day Mr. Misic -- well, our battalion command was in his house. He said to me that he needed to go and get something done at the university. He had no intention of inspecting the front-line. It was customary for us to go together when the front-line was being toured. He went to the staff, and what was said was that there were some problems. I heard that later from Drago Misic, who was also a battalion commander at the time. Then a group of Croats and representatives of the Muslims started touring the front-line there, and according to my knowledge, he was killed by bullets that had come from positions that had been held by Muslims. They later confirmed, themselves, that they had been firing, and that is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm very interested by this detail. You were saying that it is when he was touring the line with Croats and Muslims that he got killed. You said that you attended the autopsy and you noted that four different calibres of bullets hit his body. And you said -- maintained that the shots came from the Muslims. Here we've seen a large number of documents coming either from the international community or the HVO or the BH Army, where there is always mention of extremists, extremists within the HVO, extremists within the BH Army, and in many documents we have mention of these extremists. This very tragic event, notably for Mr. Tihomir Misic, might let us conclude that he was killed by Muslim extremists who were unhappy with the role he was playing and decided to shoot him on May 16, 1992. As a detail, you said that you attended the autopsy and you noted that there were four different calibres, different calibres of bullets. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the post-mortem was carried out at the Health Centre in Siroki Brijeg with regard to the wounds that were on his body. The medical team established on that occasion that the wounds were caused by 7.9-millimetre bullets, then a 7.62-millimetre bullet, then shrapnel, and some other type of ammunition that was a bit bigger, perhaps coming from a hunting gun. The autopsy also established -- or, rather, they probably noticed someone who had fired at him, or, rather, that the deceased had seen someone trying to shoot him and he probably tried to protect his face, and that is why there were wounds only on one side of his hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you about extremists, but, sir, I'm going to ask you about something that's even worse than extremists; namely: What do you know about the activities of the KOS, the infamous Counter-Intelligence Service of the former Yugoslavia, and the other secret services of Yugoslavia that were prevalently run by Communist and Serbian countries?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Counter-Intelligence Service, we know that they infiltrated their agents among all people. I think that their wish was to sow discord between the Croats and the Muslims in order to conquer the area more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's take an example. 1992 -- well, we'll be going back to 1991 as well, and the situation in Mostar is the way it is, and we'll see what it's like. But, anyway, at one point in time, someone sent information to these self-organised groups and said that they needed to have a commander. What was the name of that commander?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The groups in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, these battalions and whatever. Who was sent or appointed, in a way? Who became the so-called commander, lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Municipal Staff, Jasmin Jaganjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no. Before me. Not Jaganjac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If this is something the Chamber should hear, you must slow down, you must make a pause between question and answer. It sounds as if I said something new. Please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I must have lost my senses if yet again I could not remember to do that, Your Honour Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Before me, Witness, there is another name, Lieutenant-Colonel -- what was his name?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perak, Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Vladimir Perak. Is it correct that at one point in time, as commander of the staff, Mr. Perak ordered both the army and civilians to leave Mostar? There was shooting, and the order was to abandon Mostar; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That was at the very beginning of the month of April. The order was that all soldiers and civilians get out of Mostar, and then, subsequently, Mostar would be re-taken by military means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me if I interrupt. I'm a bit lost, I must say. At one point, Mr. Praljak asked about KOS, and you answered that they infiltrated all and aimed to divide the Croats and Muslims in order to conquer the area more easily. I take that from the transcript. Who was going to conquer which area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, KOS, the Counter-Intelligence Service that was serving the Serb people -- or the Serb aggressor, rather. That is to say that they were looking for the right kind of people among the Croats and the Muslims to conquer or take the area more easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So it would rather be the Serbs and the JNA that would conquer the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all these forces; that is to say, the JNA and these volunteers who held Mostar under siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good. And that Mr. Perak was a Serbian leader, I take. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, no. Please, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm asking the witness. I cannot ask you. I'm asking the witness. Who was Mr. Perak? Was he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think he was a Croat, but he had been infiltrated by the KOS, since he was appointed head of the Croats, the HOS [as interpreted] in Mostar. Quite simply, he cropped up as a person who wanted to help. As a lieutenant-colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, he had crossed over to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, that makes it a bit clear. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 23 says "HOS" in Mostar with an H. The witness is talking about KOS, K-O-S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] KOS, K-O-S, the Counter-Intelligence Service. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The first question. The Counter-Intelligence Service worked within which organisation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Ah. Secondly, we claimed that Perak was a Croat, that he had come from the Yugoslav People's Army, and that he became commander of the forces in Mostar, and that he ordered that Mostar be abandoned. Have we not established all of that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have established all of that, and that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you obey him, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, that order of his, that was received in the early-morning hours via radio, well, I personally had that Motorola. I woke up Tihomir Misic, and I said to him that this was something very strange. Very soon, we both agreed that that was not a good thing, and we did not transmit his order to the army. We thought that the other people from that staff were probably in danger and that something very bad was happening. Then we went to Cim, and up there we found Petar Zelenika and the others who were from the Municipal Staff. We asked what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You didn't obey him?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't obey him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You refused to carry out an order?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Where did Mr. Perak flee to after that, and where did he live after that, and where is he still living, unless he died?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best our knowledge, after that he lived somewhere in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's your answer concerning KOS, but had you obeyed Mr. Perak, whose army would have entered Mostar, whose citizens would have been in Mostar, who would have had control of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Army would enter and to take control of Mostar. In other words, they would hold the whole of Mostar under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to 1991. You said that volunteers had come, and the reservists from the Podgorica and Uzice Corps. Can you please describe to Their Honours how it was in Mostar? Were they walking around town, were they shooting, were they causing disturbance? Could anyone do anything to appease them? How was the situation in Mostar in 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time they held all the positions, all the peaks and hills around Mostar. There were frequent clashes with the civilian police. They used to drink at cafes. They would often leave without paying. There was firing often taking place. They knew, on their way to the positions, just to enter any shop and take whatever they want without paying. There was tremendous fear among all the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Jasak, and all the other people watch news at the time? Did you know what was happening in Croatia at the time, what was happening in Vukovar, Split, Zadar, Dubrovnik? Which army was attacking whom there, who was killing whom, who was shelling whom, et cetera? I'm talking about 1991. Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The attacker was also the Serbian Army. They were attacking towns in Croatia and killing people. Now that you have mentioned Dubrovnik, those were the forces from the same corps, that's to say the Titograd Corps, that were shelling it, and they were shelling it - I mean Dubrovnik - from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did anyone say anything to the citizens? Did any authority from Sarajevo, from Mostar, the government, the presidency, did they instruct them how to behave against this brutal force? Don't mention "army" now. Let's see how ordinary people felt and what the leadership was telling them. Who was leading ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ordinary people and citizens were left on their own. If you understand that Ravno was burned down in October 1991 by this very same army and that the official government, that is to say, Alija Izetbegovic, said, This is not our war, therefore there was panic everywhere and there was no organising initiative coming from the level of authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'm listening to what you are saying with great care. You are talking about official authorities. Yes, there are the official authorities, those located in Sarajevo. But as far as you know, weren't they Yugoslavian official authorities, because in 1991 Yugoslavia still existed? What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Yugoslavia did exist. But what kind of a state would be that is sending its own army against its own people? Although the village of Ravno was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was in Yugoslavia as well, and it was completely burned down and people were killed. In other words, this state of Yugoslavia didn't care about this. And the same applies to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nobody took care about those people, and that is what happened. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we are not lawyers, and we are told not to deal with these matters, but let me ask you this: From the position of Yugoslavia and the JNA, all these Muslim and Croat groups in Mostar were perceived as al-Qaeda, Tupamaros, Sendero Luminoso, Taliban. Those were insurgents against a regular state that had the right to kill its own citizens as it pleases because there was insurgency. How did you, as citizens, resolve this issue in your own minds, legally and in every other term?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We solved this in a very simple way. The only important thing for us was to organise ourselves and to try to save our lives. We did not attack anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you could see that aeroplanes were taking off from the airport on Mostar. Do you know where they went? Were they armed with rockets? Were they dropping bombs? Were they killing anyone? And if they were killing anyone, who was it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the planes took off armed with bombs and rockets and were killing the Croats in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, what happened with Ljubusko, Grude, Siroki Brijeg, Imotski, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the facilities in Grude, Siroko [as interpreted], and Ljubusko were being shelled by the Yugoslav Air Force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a little specification. You said that bombs fell and killed Croats in Croatia. That was in Croatia, not in -- I'm sorry, I didn't notice you talked about Croatia. They didn't kill Muslims, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was going on in 1991, while there was war in Croatia, while an overall war did not break out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were at the airport at the time. The military airports in Bosnia-Herzegovina were used for planes to take off to go to Croatia and to kill the population there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's right. The population, I mean, that's probably mostly Croats, but also in Croatia they were mixed ethnically, mixed communities. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's the Mostar Airport, and in 1992 they were flying over Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those places where they dropped those bombs that were outside any military important area, were there any dead women, children, and men?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were women and children and men who were killed, because residential buildings were hit as well. I know specifically a residential building in Grude, at the very entrance to Grude, was hit, because that was my municipality and I know that best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the HQ in Grude was killed [as interpreted] at Duhauska Stanica?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely the HQ at Duhauska Stanica and the building I already mentioned. This whole quarter of the town was shelled. And this station, Duhauska Stanica, was cut off by one floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into this legal issue, but in October 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared independence, and consequently Yugoslavia ceased to exist. Were you or anyone else ever invited by anyone from Sarajevo in any way whatsoever to tell you exactly and precisely what to do in the event or during such an aggression, apart from your group and apart from the fact that I later came and did things? But I'm talking about official instructions.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have never been invited to attend any meeting by any official authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1992, in April or May, what was happening in Mostar? What is the extent of the shelling? How many buildings were devastated? How many dead people were lying on the streets? Was that discriminate or indiscriminate shelling?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole town was being shelled indiscriminately and in every possible way; that is to say, already in April and May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you what happened after that because we know that, more or less. Let me just ask you this: Let's finish this issue of the road. How many local people who lived there during the war, according to your estimate, how many of these people fled because of fear and took their women and children with them?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people -- many local people fled to Croatia or to any third country, wherever they were able to find shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then who came to Mostar and where from?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever came from Mostar could only have come via Goranci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: With the arrival of the Army of Republika Srpska from Nevesinje and Bilica, who was forced to come into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim civilians from Nevesinje, Gacko, Trebinje, Bilica, and all these areas were forced into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, can you please tell Their Honours this: The vehicles that were travelling along this road, were they a permanent target of attacks by the Serbian artillery from all sides? And according to what you know, how many people died or were killed on that road?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this road, because there are many curves and one had to slow down, people were forced to drive during night without their headlights. Therefore, many people were killed on that road, because those curves were being fired at from the Hum Hill by the 76-millimetre gun with direct hits. So this 76-millimetre gun was able to fire very precisely like a sniper rifle, as they chose. They were firing all the time, and any trip in or out of town was very unsafe. Not 7.62 millimetres, but rather 76 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Two more brief questions. At the time, who was the commander of the attacking army, that is to say, of the JNA and reservists that were attacking Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the second question: After this treason by Perak and all the other things, can you tell the Chamber, when I came there, and let's take this as a hypothesis, if I issued an order to you and your late commander wouldn't agree with it, who would you listen to, to Mr. Misic or to me? I'm talking about that time.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misic, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me why.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had been with him from Day 1, because I had complete trust in him, because there was already treason committed by Perak. Therefore, I had full confidence -- or we had full confidence in our commander whom we had chosen, and he was our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then someone who was appointed as I was, you would then start obeying him not because he was appointed to that position but because he would deserve your confidence? Would that be the reason for you to later obey his orders?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very important to establish confidence in this new commander and for us to be demonstrated that he is at least as equally brave as our commander. So once the confidence is there, we would obey his orders only if and when he deserves -- or his orders deserve to be obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I apologise to everyone in the court, but I have to say this: Mr. Jasak, tell me, did I at least partly deserve this confidence because I took this road via Goranci several times during day-time, risking my life?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the most decisive factor because you were one of the few people who came into Mostar at that time and you were not a native of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I would like this to be understood only as a clarification of complicated relations in command and control, because I never spoke about this ever before this trial. Mr. Jasak, let's talk about the issue of control a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, earlier General Praljak mentioned Dubrovnik, and the question of dates is maybe a little blurry for those who may not be familiar with the history of the region and the time-line. You must be very familiar with this because you're now a top officer in the Croat army. Now, in 1991 - that was mentioned in a decision of this Court, so I'm not inventing this - was there a referendum -- would there have been a referendum in Croatia, particularly on 19th of May, 1991, and what was the result of this referendum in Croatia, and what was the referendum about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatia's independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So 90 per cent voted in favour of independence. What had happened a few months prior to that in Krajina? Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were some barricades, and this sort of Republika Srpska Krajina or something was being established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. What about the Serbian Republic of Krajina; was it established on 28th of February, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was around then. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. What about the Croatian Parliament; did it vote the independence of Croatia on the 25th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. As far as you know, what about the month of August 1991, that is to say, two months after the declaration of independence; didn't the Croats attack barracks of the JNA in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were attacks, and weapons were being taken for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you said that the Croats attacked to take weapons. The United Nations, what about the United Nations; do you know when the UN recognised the independence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Did you know what month it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, it was in May 1992. Now, before the month of May 1992, before the month of May 1992, according to you, in Dubrovnik, was Dubrovnik part of Yugoslavia, of the federation, the socialist republic, or was Dubrovnik a part of Croatia, the Croatia which was only recognised in May 1992? And so in 1991, was Dubrovnik Yugoslavian or was it Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dubrovnik was always a Croatian town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said it always was. All right. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's clarify some things. Do you remember that Iceland was the first country to recognise Croatia officially sometime in 1991? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as Croatia proclaimed its independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as independence was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Praljak. I think we should remain a bit close to the indictment, and I cannot, for the life of me, see any interest of the fact that Iceland was the first country to recognise Croatia in the context of the case we have to try. Could you perhaps ponder this and concentrate on matters that are relevant. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel. We have all been debating the fact whether a country's sovereign and independent when it declares its independence or when it stages its referendum, and when things are proclaimed by the Parliament, or whether we should have waited to be recognised by others and admitted into the UN, but let's not go that way. Let's talk about control, which is a subject important for us. We've already seen some parts of that and how that looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let me start with yourself. Did you, with any sanctions whatsoever -- were you in a position to take a suitcase, a backpack, and you and your parents, could you go towards the western part of Europe, wherever you wanted to, depending on how much money you had or whether you had relatives in Germany?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could any man do that, depending on their will and abilities, without any sanctions?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could Mr. Prlic, could Mr. Stojic, Pusic, and others, Coric, Petkovic, could they leave?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Therefore, in that area and in those groups, people who stayed were exclusively those who wanted to do so, who voluntarily stayed on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And at one point some of those groups decided that they would go under the name of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And that applied to groups in Tomislav, Livno, Ljubuski, Tomislavgrad, anywhere in the territory that the other armies did not manage to take because we had fought with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And once the war was over, was anybody punished for having left the territory, for having fled, or left, or whatever you want to call it, and had refused to be mobilised? Was anybody punished in any way for that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody was ever punished for having abandoned the territory at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jasak, later on during the war, likewise, was there a man or a group of men who could throw their arms, take off their uniforms, and take one of the hundred passages leading up to the Republic of Croatia? Was anybody sanctioned, and what sanctions were in place?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody could leave without any sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what about the arms that you had; did anybody in the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, any of its bodies, did anybody bring those arms to you and did they tell you, Okay, line up, you are now mobilised, this is your equipment, this will be your training-grounds, these are your commanders? Did any such thing happen, anything that would look like some sort of orders that the Honourable Judges know from their own states?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever did any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, now we are going to deal with two more matters. I have two maps of Mostar. I don't know whether to ask you whether to mark the positions of the Serbs. I'm asking the Judges whether they need that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that all depends on the questions you intend to ask. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've already asked the witness about the positions and where they were in 1991 and 1992, and he gave me the names of all those places. I don't know whether you want those places marked on the map or whether you already know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how my colleagues feel about it. In my personal capacity, it is extremely important to know where the Serbian positions were. Why is that? Because in the irrefutable documents from the international community -- I'm not referring to the HVO documents or from the BH Army documents, I'm referring to the documents of the international community which mentioned during the time of the indictment that the Serbs were shooting, firing, and therefore that must be taken into account. I mean, I take that into account. So if you have a map, have it put on the ELMO and ask the witness where the Serbian positions were. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 3D22 -- 3D22 -- no, 3D00730. That's one of the maps from the set, 3D22-0375.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is IC00031, the second map. The IC number is 00031. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well. That's the first map. Well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Jasak, the Usher is going to give you something to write with, and you will show us Velez Hill. Velez Hill -- please mark Velez Hill by number 1.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Encircle the whole hill and put number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole thing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And could you please just approximately mark the position of the repeater? It doesn't really matter whether you pin-point it precisely or not.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was more to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So it's off the map?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's off the map, yes. This is Hum Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark that hill by number 2.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Orlovac. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Orlovac. Stop, stop, stop. Now, tell us, please, number 2 and number 3, were those artillery positions jointly held by the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Orlovac is number 3. What about Fortica, where is that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here. [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Encircle Fortica. I didn't see you do that.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. And now put number 4 next to it.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now put a letter T, standing for "Top," T-o-p, which is "cannon." Or you can put a letter C next to the positions of their artillery. Could you put letter K, standing for "cannon."

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What about Bijelo Polje and Vrapcici? Did they have control over that area and where from? Put number 5 next to the area around Bijelo Polje and Vrapcici, number 5 around that circle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What about North Camp, number 6.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did they have mortars at number 6?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbian Army, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put letters MB.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And in this map, we can also see the only road leading out of Mostar. Can you just show us that direction and mark with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from here towards Goranci [Indicates]. No, this is not -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just give me the arrow in that direction, pointing in that direction.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So that was the direction of the only road that led out of Mostar. Thank you very much. Put today's date and your initials.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask an additional question, Witness. This situation is true for which point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time reference is the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very precise, when was the right bank of the Neretva liberated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to thank you for your contribution and the markings on this map at the request of my colleague. You said that it was at the end of 1991 and then in 1992. What I'm interested in is Mount Velez, the Velez Hill, and what you've indicated in A. My understanding is that the Serbs were there. Now, in March 1993, were they still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were up on Velez in 1993. However, here, Your Honours, I would like to have a precise topographic map. Then I could give you very precise information. This is very visually orientated because Velez is a bit to the right from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Velez is more to the right. According to you, and please listen carefully because, I mean, personally this is a question of the utmost importance, an extremely important question: In your knowledge, and it is all the more important that you're the last witness of the Petkovic Defence, and despite the fact that there will be another witness between you and Mr. Petkovic, but in theory you were planned to be the last witness, and then there will be Mr. Petkovic, and, of course, I can always ask him the question, but you are neutral because you are a simple witness. Now, please listen carefully, because I'm not going to spend hours asking questions. One question to the point which synthesizes many different issues: The guns of the Serbian artillery which were located in Velez, even though on the map you said that you'd need a topographic map, according to you, how many kilometres away were they from Mostar, East Mostar, West Mostar; how many kilometres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was some 10 to 15 kilometres. It really depended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say 10 to 15 kilometres. As far as you know, do you think that a gun which is 10 kilometres away -- let's say that we have a gun that's 15 kilometres away. You said it was 15 kilometres away. So do you think that a gun which is 15 kilometres away can shell East Mostar or West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you look at Fortica and the mortars there, I mentioned both mortars and cannons, in 1993, if we're talking about 1993, they were a bit further -- they were a bit further from Fortica. Now as I'm looking at the place where I put number 4, I know from this number 4 to Ilici, as the crow flies, we were around there, and it was some 20 kilometres or so. The distance was about 20 kilometres or so, their cannons, their artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please listen carefully. This is what I would like to know: As far as you know, you were working for Military Intelligence until August 1993, so I would like to know the following: Can a mortar or an artillery gun, a Serb mortar or Serb artillery gun, shell Mostar, the city of Mostar? It's a very simple question, but I believe that the consequences are tremendous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that in 1993, a Serb shell could reach and, indeed, did reach West Mostar, and I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If it could reach West Mostar, could it also reach East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is all I wanted to know. Mr. Praljak, the Registrar is telling me that you have used 45 minutes so far. I know that you had 30 minutes, and the Prlic Defence gave you their 30 minutes. In such a case, you have 14 minutes left. But I know that the counsels for Defence had some questions to put, so I don't know -- your counsel also had questions to put, so how are you going to share that time? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll go on until I finish some of my questions, and then we'll see where we stand. Let's clarify some things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. First the Registrar must give us a number for this map, because we've lost track of things. Mr. Registrar, we need an IC number. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have something else to add? Go ahead, Mr. Praljak. You say that you want to use up all of your time. I mean, you are the ones giving instructions to your counsel. You know, an accused can give instruction to his counsel, of course, which means that if Ms. Pinter runs out of time, well, it's too bad for her because you will have used up all the time for yourself. That's the way it works; right? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Here's a very simple question, sir. Number 4 in the map, Fortica, even after 1992 and 1993, was there an artillery position of the Army of Republika Srpska there? And I'm talking about a mortar, 76 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an artillery position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We can easily see how far that is from anywhere else, and we will not talk about that. The second question, sir: Judge Antonetti asked you whether the Serbian artillery could hit West Mostar. Would East Mostar be even closer to the Serbian artillery than West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: East Mostar is closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So if they could hit Western Mostar, they could also hit Eastern Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I apologise. I should finish. Yes, okay, that was that. And now let's look at the next map, which is IC0031 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll give a number to this map. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked version of document 3D00730 shall be given Exhibit IC01165. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] IC00031 is the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away, Mr. Jasak, this is the southern part of Mostar. First we were looking at the northern part of Mostar, and now we are looking at the northern part of Mostar and almost the whole of southern Mostar. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, no, this should be changed. IC00031 is the one that I asked for. It's already an exhibit. 3DT -- I don't know. Ms. Pinter, please help.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that was the IC00031. That's the IC number. Now we have it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, now we have it. It's upside down. There we have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please disregard the inscriptions on the map, and again could you do the same thing as you did before? First of all, could you please mark Velez once again? Velez and Fortica as well.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There you have them, Velez --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And circle the entire mountain. Encircle Velez.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But now it's the other way around. It's completely upside down. I have north in the left and now I have south in the upper part. I don't know how I should be looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We're looking at the map as if we were in the north. Do you see the airport? Take your time, find your bearings. Can you put number 1, please?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, that's -- I understand now. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you now mark the Southern Camp? Use the letters JL.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now could you please mark Hum? Put number 3 next to Hum.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's that.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's completely upside down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please mark Orlovac.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orlovac, number 4. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark Velez, mountain Velez.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Completely, completely. Circle it completely. Velez is a big mountain. Okay. That was number 5. And now could you please mark Fortica on Mount Velez and put number 6 next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now could you please show us where the repeater was and put number 7 next to it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now mark the position of Heliodrom and put number 8 next to it.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now Sokol and Glinica. Sokol will be number 9. Glinica will be number 10.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. To the right from number 8 is Sokol, of course. Just take your time.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 9 and this is 10, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay, well.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the middle is Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just roughly, where was Cula, the big transformer, electricity transformer facility somewhere around Hum?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay. Put number 11 next to it. Never mind. And now, Mr. Jasak, tell us, please, first of all, let's identify the date when we chased those units away from the right bank of the Neretva to the left of the Neretva. So when did we liberate the right bank? Could you please show us -- we see the Neretva flowing here. Could you please show us the direction in which the Neretva flows, and put an arrow next to West Mostar. Could you please show us where West Mostar was, and can we have an arrow marked with a W, and then East marked with an E.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: There you go. And now tell the Trial Chamber what was the date when we liberated the right bank of the River Neretva.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right bank of the River Neretva, we liberated it on the 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the east bank?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later, on the 14th and the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: June?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now please tell us, where on Velez -- on what positions did the Army of Republika Srpska stay throughout the entire time? Which positions did they hold, Fortica, Podvelezje, and others, where were they throughout the entire war and even before and after the conflict that started between the HVO and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that maybe Usher could give another colour to the pencil. I believe we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like this? [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: VRS, write that.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And my last question as regards this map: On oppositions from this front-line, on one side and the other side, could they have their artillery and did they?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have artillery, and it would be hard for me to mark their artillery now because this is not a topographic map so I cannot do it accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The last question in relation to this map. Throughout the war, even during the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, did Serb artillery hit the right and left bank of Mostar whenever they wanted to in order to cause a conflict between the two sides and also because they liked it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were firing at Mostar all the time, and that is contained in our reports from the VOS service, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina paid the Serbs to hit us when they would start attacking? You were in the VOS. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of such information. I mentioned that earlier on. They also procured weapons from them, and I even think that that attack on the 9th of May, that at that time also this was shelling that had been ordered or commissioned. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could I please have an IC number for this map, and could you mark it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar will give you an IC number. And I have a very simple question to ask you after that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked version of IC00031 shall be given Exhibit IC01166. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, three of the four Judges that you have here on the Bench have been to Mostar. We know the area, we're familiar with the area, so we know what the topography is like. You, in red, you gave us an indication of where the VRS was located, and you said that this applied for 1993. I note -- and if I'm wrong, please tell me. I note -- what is the map -- why has it disappeared? I'm asking you a very important question, and everything disappeared simultaneously. It's all gone. Registrar, could we please recall the map with the markings. My question -- I have to put my question with the map, with the marked map on the screen. Very well, now it's back on the screen. In this courtroom, everyone can see this map, including the Prosecutor. Everybody can see that in 1993, according to the witness, anyway - I wasn't there in 1993, but the witness was there at least until August - well, he says that in 1993 the Serb positions were as marked on the map in red. I note that right under these Serb positions, we have East Mostar, where the Muslims resided at the time. Witness, from the Serb position as we see it on the map, was it easy to shoot at East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was easy to fire wherever they wanted to fire, including East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would -- with your permission, I would like to ask a few questions with regard to this allegation that the ABiH paid the Serbs for shelling the Croats. In a simplified way, I put it. For what time-span would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no way of knowing which shell was paid for and came from Serb territory or Muslim territory. I don't know how long that lasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe there was an error in translation. I did, of course, not ask about any single shells. You have confirmed that the Muslim side, ABiH, gave money to the Serbs in exchange of the Serbs shelling the Croats, and I would like to know to which period in time you are referring. Is this between 1991 and 1995, or only in a part of that period, and which one would it be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only meant May/June, roughly, 1993, somewhere around then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And a question you have been asked frequently. How do you know? On what is your answer based? Have you seen documents? Have you spoken with people who paid or with people who received payment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is based on the knowledge that we received from the field and that was contained in our reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So it is intelligence that you gathered from the enemy side surreptitiously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is information that we, that is to say, our personnel, gathered on the ground and submitted that to VOS. VOS did have such information available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you be a bit more precise about the volume of the payment, the link between payment and shelling? Was it, for instance, I order 50 shells on Podhum and I'm prepared to pay 20.000 Deutchemark, something of that? Do you have such precise information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our information was only that they paid a lot of money for that. I cannot say exactly how much, but I know that it was very expensive, on the basis of the information that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have two more documents that I would like to deal with quickly, and then I'll deal with yet another question. 3D00420, have a look at that. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Take a look. This a decision on the formation of Territorial Defence units that was signed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic on the 27th of May, 1992. My first question: On the 27th of May, 1992, was the entire population of the eastern part of Mostar expelled or, rather, had they been expelled 10 days earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska or, rather, the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there any casualties then? Were people killed, wounded?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who were killed and wounded, and we know that whatever had stayed on, as far as the military component is concerned, these people were trained at our military centre in Goranci. We took them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Everything we heard about the 27th of May, 1992, was -- well, you see the president of the Presidency is establishing a territorial defence. First of all, this Krajl Tomislav Brigade, with General Mate Sarlija Daidza, as its command, is that the first -- I'll repeat the question slowly. This unit and General Sarlija, were they a unit of the Croatian Army up until then?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit, as a volunteer brigade called Krajl Tomislav, did exist in Croatia, and Mate Sarlija Daidza was its commander. And this brigade stopped the breakthrough of the Serb forces towards Dubrovnik and Cene Kuca [phoen], that is to say, their breakthrough towards the sea, the coast. That is the unit that had stopped that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, there are 39 commanders here. First of all, tell me -- have a look at this. Is there any locality here from Herzegovina, East/West Mostar, Ljubuski, Tomislavgrad --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: -- Prozor, Jablanica? Is there anything here that has to do with what the HVO has already fighting? The HVO was fighting well and strongly. Can you find a single locality where it was the HVO that was fighting?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had a look at this, and I cannot find a single locality where the HVO was operating; only Brcko, Tuzla, TO --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: There are no units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there is no need for him to be appointed in an army that is defending Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is fighting well and properly; is that the explanation for this document?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the absolutely logical explanation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at document P04 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it may not be crystal clear for a people who need to have a long explanation before they understand. I mean, this is a document which I see for the first time. Personally, I did not know it until now, so I'm finding out about it. And within just a few seconds, I must have a quick look at the 39 names, 39 brigades, to know whether there are TOs in the Croatian zone. You say, No. Well, of course this is a big problem, because this is a document dated from May 1992, the president of the Presidency himself signs it, and he creates the Territorial Defence, i.e., the territorial defences for all of the territories in the republic. And here, obviously, some are missing. So couldn't an explanation be that at this time, in his mind, the territorial defences in which Croats are located are enough, and he didn't think that it was necessary for him to include them because, according to him, they were legal and it was pointless to quote them? What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the only logical thing for me here is the following: In those areas that are not included in this decision, there is already an impeccable defence that is in place and that all necessary activities had already been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the perfectly or well-organised defence, that the measure was the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Praljak, as you know, we are only going to take one break today. It's almost time for the break. We are going to take now a 20-minute break. Please see with your counsel how much time you have left, to avoid any problem. And apparently it looks like you are getting close to one hour already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, here's a decision of the Trial Chamber. As you know, the Prosecution has recorded a filing about the granting of time that it requests for the cross-examination of Witness 4D-AA. In other words, the Prosecution would like to have two hours as a whole, in total. Because of that, the Trial Chamber would like to ask Defence counsels to inform it of their positions prior to Wednesday, 27th of February, 2010, midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are just working on that, and it will be filed before -- on Wednesday, at latest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, regarding the time allocation, I'd like to thank the Registrar for his calculations. The Chamber had granted three hours to the five teams of counsel. Three hours, that's 180 minutes. Divided by 5, that is 36 minutes per team. So Mr. Praljak had the 36 minutes at his disposal, because the Prlic Defence gave him his 36 minutes. Because of you've already used up 51 minutes, Mr. Praljak, you have another 21 minutes left from this very moment, so for you and Ms. Pinter. So, Witness, I only have one follow-on question, if I may. The question is complex and the Trial Chamber in its decision will say -- mention the dates recognition of Croatia and so on. But for our understanding, did you know that on the 15th of January, 2002, in Zagreb, there were ceremonies about the 10th anniversary of the international recognition, ceremonies presided over by the president of your republic, Mr. Mesic, and that during that day, the 15th of January, 2002, there was one coin of 25 kuna which was made about the recognition of the European Union the 25th of January, 2002? So apparently your authorities state the date of recognition as the 15th of January, 1992, if I refer to this event, given that General Praljak was right in saying that Iceland was the first one to recognise -- did recognise Croatia, but it was not the first country, it was Slovenia on the 26th of June, then came Lithuania, and Iceland recognised it on 19th of December, 1991. So did you know, Witness, that your authorities had an official ceremony on the 15th of January, 2002, saying that it was a celebration of the 10th anniversary of the recognition by the European community? Maybe you know it, maybe you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one cautionary note, Mr. President. If you could speak a little slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I felt that the witness speaks French. So did you understand the question, sir? Otherwise, you know, I can repeat it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood your question in general, and I am aware that it is necessary to celebrate a recognition by the UN, but I also don't think that the Croatian Parliament did not take a decision that was not legitimate and that was not based on the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Yes, absolutely. Thank you very much. Mr. Praljak, over to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, we said -- P06482, it's a document, and there was one question unresolved relating to a meeting held on the 7th of November, 1993, in Tomislavgrad. Do you recognise my signature, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise your signature, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it abundantly clear from this document that by virtue of my right to convene this meeting, I did convene it for the 7th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is apparent and obvious from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, you left for Zagreb. Can you tell the Judges, did you forget that you hailed from Mostar after you moved to Zagreb? Did you call us by telephone? Were you interested in what problems we were having and facing? Did you remain in Mostar spiritually?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only spiritually. I used to come to Mostar from Zagreb nearly every weekend because my girlfriend at the time lived in Mostar. That is to say, I came to Mostar nearly every weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many children do you have with this girlfriend of yours who is now your wife?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have five children, and that girlfriend of mine is my wife now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, given the problems of the functioning of a state - let us not go into the problems dealing with electricity, water supply, et cetera - isn't something completely natural for a commander to convene a meeting with his subordinate commanders and personnel and tell them exactly what needs to be done in order to avoid losing a war? Isn't that something which is completely natural and normal; maybe not in the US Army, maybe not in the Foreign Legion; but in the situation that prevailed at the time, wasn't that an only logical and correct approach?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the same thing yesterday. I can absolutely understand that. I didn't know it was you who convened that meeting, but now I realise that that was the most natural thing to do under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look at another thing, please. Is this addressed to the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It clearly says that this is to -- addressed to the commander of South-Eastern Herzegovina Military District; Western Herzegovina Military District; and two professional units, Bruno Busic Regiment and Ludvig Pavlovic Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We're finished with this document. And now, Mr. Jasak and Your Honours, please understand me. We need to clarify the system of communication and the possibility of eavesdropping. I also refer to Paket communications. Mr. Jasak is also a mechanical engineer, but I would be most happy to put me in the dock and to question me about how the whole situation was, but regrettably things are not going the way that I would like to see them going. I would like the truth to come out, and I will try now to resolve certain issues with Mr. Jasak. Regardless of where the Main Staff and their headquarters was, was always a room with a device that is called Paket communications device. Can you describe it for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a computer and a Hamm operator's radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: A Hamm operator's radio station means that -- does it mean that roughly between 144 and 146 megahertz frequency is being used, that is, two metres of the wavelength?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two metres' wavelength.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Slowly, slowly. So 144 to 146 megahertz frequency; and wavelength, two metres.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, these frequencies are used by old [as interpreted] Hamm operators. They listen to each other, and they are using Morse code to communicate with one another?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And it's the same today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. Now, what is the difference? Can one say that this is a relatively secure communication line? Because, you know, one can easily listen to Hamm operators. You can just change the entry impedance. Was it actually the computer that was the crucial part?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So this computer converts a written text into a digital signal and it adds certain numerals, so it is dispatching bits like 000111, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, this digital system of conversion of what we want to transmit is much more difficult to detect than the analogue system?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And if, in addition to that, we do the encryption through the computer by adding additional bits under the code known only by the sender and the receiver, then we have considerably well protected our message; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, because the enemy could receive a message, but it was useless because they couldn't decipher it, since it was encrypted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A question of the transcript, please, before it disappears. If you look at page 43, line 2, we read that: "The frequencies were used by old Hamm operators." I suspect that what you wanted to say and perhaps said was "all Hamm operators." I invite you to speak up so that it comes into the transcript, because even if you nod in a very friendly way, as you just did, the paper will not take it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for you, Honourable Judge, to finish, because if I interrupt you, you are going to criticise me again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That might be a point, but I had, in fact, finished. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, I said all Hamm operators used that, even today, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Of course, would you agree with me, Mr. Jasak, that on the opposite side that is listening in, there is an American or a French service of detection trying to break our code with very powerful computer programmes? Were they able to do that in about 20 hours?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you have extremely powerful technology, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: But on the opposite side there were people who didn't have such powerful computers capable of processing extremely quickly the data received and of breaking the code under which we were sending our messages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, we managed that once a month, change the code in all those stations at an agreed time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. If the conditions were regular, this was changed; but if there was a case of a station being captured, the code was changed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay, let's move on. Let's say in Mostar someone sends a message. Oh, let's establish one more thing. And in this message you have lower-case letters, upper-case letters, colons, commas, and full stops, and these signs were converted into a signal, which only makes it clear that no signature could have been transmitted in that way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on. In that room in Mostar, you said there was a Paket communications system. Was there the same system existing in the zone where Lasic was?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was there one in Grude?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the brigade. Well, but for some reason somebody from Central Bosnia can, by using the repeater, send a message to Mate Boban more easily by coming to this control room and use this device that is housed at the HQ. What will the person who receives such a message do? Is he going to put a stamp on this message received from the staff and say, Received?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he would do. And then he would put this message in an envelope and deliver it to the office of President Boban, who was at Rondo, where Mr. Vucina, who was the head of his office, was also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that was my next question. This message, therefore, didn't go to the chief of the Main Staff, or the commander of the Main Staff, or to the Main Staff at all; it goes, rather, to the recipient, just like any other letter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So if we would receive a message in a Main Staff addressed to His Honour Judge Trechsel, we would convey or deliver this message to him without reading it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it will be put in an envelope, a sealed envelope, and it would be addressed to the Judge. And the only persons who had the opportunity to see it were the operator. It would not go to the office of the chief of Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
